q: Compare the relaxed sarcomere with the contracted one. Which part keeps the same width?
options: The I band
The H zone
The A band
The distance between Z discs

why.correct: The A band is the length of the thick filaments, and the thick filaments do not change length. The thin filaments slide in over them, so the A band keeps its width while everything defined by a gap narrows.
options: The I bands are clearly narrower in the contracted sarcomere, because thick filaments now reach farther toward the Z discs.
The H zone has almost vanished, because the thin filaments from both ends now nearly meet.
Correct. The A band, the thick filaments' length, is unchanged.
The Z discs are closer together; that is the shortening of the sarcomere.

q: Starting with a cocked myosin head holding ADP and phosphate, put one turn of the cross-bridge cycle in order.
options: The head binds an uncovered site on actin
Phosphate is released and the head pivots in the power stroke
ADP is released at the end of the stroke
A new ATP binds and the head lets go of actin
The head splits ATP and returns to the cocked position

why.correct: The cocked head binds actin, forming a cross-bridge. Releasing phosphate drives the power stroke, and ADP leaves at its end, leaving the head tightly bound. A new ATP binding makes it let go, and splitting that ATP recocks it for the next turn.

q: A few hours after death, ATP in the muscle fibers has run out. Predict the change in each variable, compared with a living, relaxed muscle.

variables.name: Myosin heads detaching from actin
variables.why: A head lets go of actin only when a new ATP binds it; with no ATP, attached heads stay attached.

variables.name: Number of cross-bridges attached
variables.why: Calcium leaking into the sarcoplasm uncovers actin, heads bind and complete their stroke, and none can detach.

variables.name: Stiffness of the muscle
variables.why: Locked cross-bridges bolt the thick and thin filaments together, so the muscle cannot be stretched.

variables.name: Calcium pumped into the SR
variables.why: The SR calcium pumps are ATPases; without ATP they stop.

why.correct: Without ATP, the cross-bridge cycle stops after the power stroke. Heads that bind actin cannot let go, the calcium pumps fail so the binding sites stay uncovered, and the locked filaments make the muscles stiff: rigor mortis.

q: An experimental drug lets ATP bind to myosin heads but stops them from splitting it. A fiber treated with the drug is then stimulated. What happens?
options: The fiber stays relaxed and easily stretched, because the heads let go but cannot recock
The fiber goes into rigor, because the heads cannot let go of actin
The fiber contracts normally, because ATP binding powers the stroke
The fiber contracts and cannot relax, because calcium stays on troponin

why.correct: Binding ATP is what releases a head from actin, so the heads detach. But splitting ATP is what recocks them, so they never return to the high-energy position needed to bind and pull. No cross-bridges cycle, no force develops, and the muscle stays slack.
options: Correct. Detachment works; recocking does not.
Rigor needs heads stuck on actin with no ATP bound. Here ATP binds, so the heads come off.
The power stroke uses energy stored in the cocked head from an earlier split. Binding alone releases the head; it does not power a stroke.
The drug acts on myosin, not on the SR calcium pumps, so calcium is still cleared after stimulation.

q: A sarcomere is 2.2 µm long, and its thick filaments are 1.6 µm long. What is the total width of its I band (both halves added together)?
options: 1.6 µm
0.6 µm
3.8 µm
0.2 µm

why.correct: The I band is the part of the sarcomere not covered by thick filaments: 2.2 − 1.6 = 0.6 µm, split as 0.3 µm on each side of the sarcomere.
options: 1.6 µm is the width of the A band, which equals the thick filament length.
Correct. Sarcomere length minus A band: 2.2 − 1.6 = 0.6 µm.
This adds the two lengths instead of subtracting; the I band must be shorter than the sarcomere.
This comes from subtracting two thin filament lengths (2 × 1.0 µm), which gives the H zone if the thin filaments are 1.0 µm long, not the I band.

q: In a muscle whose thin filaments each reach 1.0 µm in from their Z disc, a sarcomere shortens from 2.4 µm to 2.1 µm. What happens to the width of its H zone?
options: It stays at 0.4 µm
It widens from 0.1 µm to 0.4 µm
It narrows from 1.4 µm to 1.1 µm
It narrows from 0.4 µm to 0.1 µm

why.correct: The H zone is the part of the sarcomere the thin filaments from the two ends do not reach: sarcomere length − 2 × 1.0 µm. Before: 2.4 − 2.0 = 0.4 µm. After: 2.1 − 2.0 = 0.1 µm.
options: The H zone depends on how far the thin filaments slide in, so it changes as the sarcomere shortens.
This reverses before and after; more overlap makes the H zone narrower, not wider.
These values subtract only one thin filament length, but thin filaments reach in from both ends.
Correct. 0.4 µm narrows to 0.1 µm as the thin filaments slide toward each other.

q: Paramedics find a man who died about eight hours ago. His jaw and elbows cannot be moved. What is holding his muscles stiff?
options: Continuous action potentials in his muscle fibers
Myosin heads bound to actin that cannot detach without ATP
Acetylcholine left bound to the end plates
Tropomyosin locked over the binding sites on actin

why.correct: After death, ATP runs out. Calcium leaks into the sarcoplasm and uncovers actin, heads bind and complete their stroke, and without ATP to bind them they cannot let go. The locked cross-bridges hold the filaments together: rigor mortis.
options: Nerves and muscle membranes stop firing after death; the stiffness is in the filaments, not the membranes.
Correct. Rigor is locked cross-bridges.
Acetylcholine acts only on the end plate's channels; it does not hold filaments together.
Covered binding sites would leave the muscle relaxed and easy to stretch, the opposite of rigor.

q: In the cross-bridge cycle, what makes a myosin head let go of actin?
options: Release of phosphate from the head
Calcium leaving troponin
A new ATP molecule binding to the head
Splitting of ATP into ADP and phosphate

why.correct: Binding of a fresh ATP changes the head's shape so it no longer grips actin. Splitting the ATP comes afterward and recocks the head.
options: Phosphate release goes with the power stroke, while the head is still attached.
Calcium leaving troponin stops new heads from binding, but a head already attached still needs ATP to let go.
Correct. ATP binding releases the head.
Splitting ATP recocks a head that has already let go.

q: Select every change that happens when a sarcomere contracts.
options: The Z discs move closer together
The I bands narrow
The A band narrows
The H zone narrows
The thin filaments get shorter
The overlap of thick and thin filaments increases

why.correct: Thin filaments slide toward the M line, so overlap increases, the Z discs are pulled closer, and the I bands and H zone, which are gaps between filaments, narrow. The A band and the filaments themselves keep their lengths.
options: Correct. The thin filaments are anchored to the Z discs and pull them inward.
Correct. The thick filaments now reach closer to the Z discs.
The A band is the length of the thick filaments, which does not change.
Correct. The thin filaments from both ends move toward each other.
Filaments slide; neither kind shortens.
Correct. Sliding increases the overlap.

q: A student wrote out the cross-bridge cycle. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: A cocked head holding ADP and phosphate binds actin
Phosphate is released and the head pivots, pulling the thin filament toward the M line
ADP is released and the head stays bound
Splitting of ATP makes the head let go of actin
The energy of split ATP recocks the head

why.correct: It is the binding of a new ATP, not its splitting, that makes the head let go. Splitting happens after detachment and recocks the head.
options: This step is right. The cocked head binds an uncovered site, forming a cross-bridge.
This step is right. This is the power stroke.
This step is right. After ADP leaves, the head is tightly bound until ATP arrives.
This is the error. ATP binding, not splitting, detaches the head.
This step is right. Hydrolysis energy resets the head to its high-energy position.

q: Fill the gap: a myosin head attached to actin, linking a thick filament to a thin one, is called a ____.
options: Z disc
Cross-bridge
Triad
Power stroke

why.correct: A cross-bridge is a myosin head bound to actin. It exists only while the head is attached.
options: A Z disc anchors thin filaments at the ends of a sarcomere.
Correct. The head bridges across to the thin filament.
A triad is a T tubule with two terminal cisternae.
The power stroke is the pivot a cross-bridge makes, not the attached head itself.

q: Early researchers found that during contraction the A band keeps its width while the I band narrows. Why did this rule out the idea that the filaments themselves shorten?
options: The A band is made of thin filaments, which would have to lengthen
The I band contains the thick filaments, so its narrowing shows they slide
The A band is the length of the thick filaments, so a constant A band means the thick filaments did not shorten
Filaments made of protein cannot change length

why.correct: The A band spans the thick filaments from end to end. If the thick filaments shortened, the A band would narrow. Because it stays the same while the I band shrinks, the thin filaments must be sliding in over thick filaments of constant length.
options: The A band is set by the thick filaments; the thin filaments reach into it from the ends.
The I band contains thin filaments only.
Correct. A constant A band means constant thick filaments.
Some proteins do change shape; the evidence here comes from the bands, not from a rule about proteins.

q: Why do the thin filaments on both sides of a sarcomere move toward its center, rather than all in the same direction?
options: The myosin heads on the two halves of each thick filament point in opposite directions
The Z discs pull the thin filaments inward
Calcium is released only at the center of the sarcomere
The thin filaments on one side are made of a different protein

why.correct: The heads on each half of a thick filament point away from the M line, mirror images of each other. Every power stroke pulls a thin filament toward the M line, so the two sets of thin filaments, and the Z discs they are anchored to, move inward from both ends.
options: Correct. The mirror-image arrangement of the heads sets the direction.
The Z discs are pulled by the thin filaments; they do not pull on their own.
Calcium is released from terminal cisternae at the triads and spreads through the whole sarcomere.
Thin filaments on both sides are built from the same actin, troponin and tropomyosin.

q: Where is the energy from splitting ATP held just before the power stroke?
options: In the bond between the myosin head and actin
In the calcium bound to troponin
In a new ATP molecule waiting to bind the head
In the cocked, high-energy shape of the myosin head

why.correct: Splitting ATP recocks the head into a bent, high-energy position, like setting a mousetrap. The power stroke releases that stored energy as movement, after the head binds actin and lets go of its phosphate.
options: Binding actin triggers the stroke, but the energy was stored in the head's shape before it bound.
Calcium acts as a switch that uncovers the binding sites; it does not supply energy for the stroke.
A new ATP binds after the stroke and releases the head; its energy is used for the next recocking.
Correct. The energy is stored in the cocked head.

q: In a living muscle fiber with plenty of ATP, calcium in the sarcoplasm stays high because the SR calcium pumps have been blocked. Predict the change in each variable, compared with a fiber whose pumps work.

variables.name: Binding sites on actin left uncovered
variables.why: With calcium staying on troponin, tropomyosin stays off the binding sites.

variables.name: Cross-bridge cycling
variables.why: ATP is available, so heads keep binding, pulling, detaching and recocking for as long as the sites are uncovered.

variables.name: Time the fiber stays contracted
variables.why: Relaxation needs calcium to leave troponin, and the pumps that would lower it are blocked.

variables.name: Number of heads locked on actin as in rigor
variables.why: Rigor needs a lack of ATP. Here ATP binds and releases each head, so the heads keep cycling rather than locking.

why.correct: Two conditions keep the cycle running: calcium on troponin and ATP. With calcium kept high and ATP present, the heads keep cycling and the fiber stays contracted. That is a sustained contraction, not rigor, because every head can still let go.

q: Two days after a death, the body's muscles are limp again, although no ATP has returned. What ends rigor mortis?
options: Calcium is pumped back into the SR
The myosin heads recock and let go
Enzymes inside the dead cells break down the proteins holding the filaments together
New ATP is made by anaerobic respiration

why.correct: Rigor passes off over one to three days as enzymes released inside the dead fibers break down the muscle proteins. The locked cross-bridges are not released; the structure they hold together falls apart.
options: The pumps need ATP, and there is none; calcium does not return to the SR after death.
Letting go requires ATP to bind, and recocking requires ATP to be split; neither is available.
Correct. Protein breakdown, not cross-bridge release, ends rigor.
Anaerobic breakdown of glycogen stops within hours of death, before rigor is even complete.

q: A myofibril has 20,000 sarcomeres in series. Each one shortens by 0.4 µm. How much does the myofibril shorten?
options: 0.8 cm
8 cm
0.4 µm

why.correct: Sarcomeres in series add their shortening: 20,000 × 0.4 µm = 8,000 µm. Since 1 cm = 10,000 µm, that is 0.8 cm.
options: Correct. 8,000 µm = 0.8 cm.
This treats 1 cm as 1,000 µm; 1 cm is 10,000 µm.
Every sarcomere shortens by 0.4 µm, and in series their shortenings add; the whole myofibril shortens far more.
This treats 1 cm as 100,000 µm; 1 cm is 10,000 µm.
The binding of ATP that frees the myosin head
The pivot of an attached myosin head that pulls the thin filament toward the M line
The release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
The action potential that spreads down the T tubules

why.correct: In the power stroke, a myosin head bound to actin releases its phosphate and pivots at its hinge, dragging the thin filament a few nanometers toward the M line.
options: ATP binding is the detachment step that follows the stroke.
Correct. The pivot of the attached head is the power stroke.
Calcium release is part of excitation–contraction coupling, which allows the cycle to start.
The action potential is the electrical signal that starts the whole sequence, not a movement of myosin.
